content:
The following Motion was moved and
seconded.
 
"Council notes
that:
-           
Motor neurone disease (MND) is a rapidly progressing condition
– a third of people die within a year of diagnosis and half
within two years. As the disease progresses, symptoms worsen and
needs increase, often unpredictably.
-           
People living with progressive or terminal conditions like MND
deserve to live in safe, accessible homes. They have the right to
independence and quality of life in the time they have
left.
-           
It is our council’s role to ensure that local people
living with MND and other progressive or terminal illnesses are
supported to access the home adaptations they need in a timely
manner.
-           
Without timely support, people face becoming trapped in
unsuitable and unsafe homes. This risks significant negative
impacts on their health and well-being, including increased risk of
avoidable hospital admissions and early entry into care.
-           
The MND Association has proposed a set of recommendations and
highlighted examples of good practice in their report, A Lifeline
Not a Luxury.
-           
One such recommendation is to speed up applications for the
funding and installation of home adaptations. This would be hugely
beneficial for people living with MND, who could live safely at
home for longer, maintain their health and wellbeing for as long as
possible, and remain engaged with their communities, family and
friends.
-           
People living with MND do not have time to wait – every
day is critical. This council recognises that people with
progressive conditions should be able to apply for adaptations as
early as possible following diagnosis, so that their future needs
can be anticipated rather than responded to in crisis.
-           
This council also recognises that early interventions can save
taxpayer money by enabling people to manage their condition more
effectively and reducing the need for critical interventions at a
later stage.
-           
West Lancashire Borough Council's current target timeframe is 83
working days for High Priority cases and 151 working days for
Standard Priority cases, with longer timeframes for complex
work.
Council
therefore:
-           
Supports in principle that residents living with progressive or
terminal conditions such as MND should automatically be treated as
High Priority for the purposes of home adaptation
assessments.
-           
Requests that officers review current target timeframes for home
adaptations. For residents with progressive or terminal conditions
who are classified as High Priority, the aim should be to achieve
the MND Association's recommended timescales of 55 days for simple
adaptations and no more than 130 days for complex
adaptations.
-           
Recognises that these targets should be seen as a maximum, and
for many smaller adaptations such as ramps or stairlifts the
expectation would be to move much faster.
-           
Requests that the findings of this review, including any
recommendations for changes to policy, targets, or processes, be
reported to the relevant committee as soon as practicable."
 
A vote was taken, the Motion was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.   
That it be noted that:
(i)       
Motor neurone disease (MND) is a rapidly progressing condition
– a third of people die within a year of diagnosis and half
within two years. As the disease progresses, symptoms worsen and
needs increase, often unpredictably.
(ii)      
People living with progressive or terminal conditions like MND
deserve to live in safe, accessible homes. They have the right to
independence and quality of life in the time they have left.
(iii)    
It is our council’s role to ensure that local people living
with MND and other progressive or terminal illnesses are supported
to access the home adaptations they need in a timely manner.
(iv)    
Without timely support, people face becoming trapped in unsuitable
and unsafe homes. This risks significant negative impacts on their
health and well-being, including increased risk of avoidable
hospital admissions and early entry into care.
(v)     
The MND Association has proposed a set of recommendations and
highlighted examples of good practice in their report, A
Lifeline Not a Luxury.
(vi)    
One such recommendation is to speed up applications for the funding
and installation of home adaptations. This would be hugely
beneficial for people living with MND, who could live safely at
home for longer, maintain their health and wellbeing for as long as
possible, and remain engaged with their communities, family and
friends.
(vii)  
People living with MND do not have time to wait – every day
is critical. This council recognises that people with progressive
conditions should be able to apply for adaptations as early as
possible following diagnosis, so that their future needs can be
anticipated rather than responded to in crisis.
(viii) 
This council also recognises that early interventions can save
taxpayer money by enabling people to manage their condition more
effectively and reducing the need for critical interventions at a
later stage.
(ix)    
West Lancashire Borough Council's current target timeframe is 83
working days for High Priority cases and 151 working days for
Standard Priority cases, with longer timeframes for complex
work.
 

B.   
That residents living with progressive or terminal conditions such
as MND be supported in principal and be automatically treated as
High Priority for the purposes of home adaptation assessments.
 

That officers review current target
timeframes for home adaptations and for residents with progressive
or terminal conditions who are classified as High Priority, the aim
should be to achieve the MND Association's recommended timescales
of 55 days for simple adaptations and no more than 130 days
for complex adaptations.

 

That these targets should be seen as
a maximum, and for many smaller adaptations such as ramps or
stairlifts the expectation would be to move much faster.

 

That the findings of the review,
including any recommendations for changes to policy, targets, or
processes, be reported to the relevant committee as soon as
practicable.
topline: The Council has decided to prioritize residents with progressive or terminal conditions like MND for home adaptations to ensure timely support and independence.

content:
The following Motion was moved and seconded as
follows:
 
"This Council notes that:

The Government’s English Devolution White
Paper – Power and Partnership: Foundations for Growth
(December 2024) sets out the most significant programme of local
government reform in over fifty years, combining Local Government
Reorganisation with English devolution. The White Paper makes clear
that these reforms are intended not only to simplify local
government but also to strengthen local democracy and community
empowerment.
The White Paper states:

“We know people value the role of
governance at the community scale… We will therefore want to
see stronger community arrangements when reorganisation
happens… We will also rewire the relationship between town
and parish councils and principal local authorities, strengthening
expectations on engagement and community voice.”

The Government has made clear that larger unitary
authorities should be complemented by stronger community
governance, ensuring that local identity and neighbourhood
representation are strengthened rather than
diminished.
Skelmersdale and Ormskirk are West
Lancashire’s two principal towns, each with its own distinct
history, identity, communities and aspirations, yet neither
benefits from an elected town council dedicated solely to
representing its residents and championing its local
priorities.
Skelmersdale is one of England’s largest
towns without a town council, while Ormskirk, the Borough’s
historic market town and administrative centre, likewise lacks an
elected town council despite its significant civic, cultural and
economic importance.
Town councils across England play an increasingly
important role in:



representing local communities;
supporting regeneration and economic
development;
delivering neighbourhood services;
managing community assets;
supporting local organisations;
improving parks and public spaces;
promoting civic pride and local
identity.


This Council believes that:
Local Government Reorganisation must
strengthen—not weaken—local democracy.
As decision-making moves to larger
unitary authorities serving substantially larger populations, there
is a compelling need to ensure that communities continue to have a
strong, democratic voice at the neighbourhood level.
The creation of Town Councils for both
Skelmersdale and Ormskirk would provide that voice by creating
democratically accountable bodies focused exclusively on the
interests of their respective communities.
Such councils would:

strengthen local democracy and
accountability;
enhance community engagement and
participation;
support regeneration and economic
development;
promote civic identity and local
pride;
provide stronger advocacy for local
communities;
work in partnership with the future unitary
authority to deliver neighbourhood priorities;
ensure that decisions affecting each town continue
to be shaped by those who know and represent them
best.

The Council further believes that the
current programme of Local Government Reorganisation presents a
once-in-a-generation opportunity to establish governance
arrangements that will serve the people of West Lancashire for
decades to come.
This Council therefore resolves to:

Commence a Community Governance Review under the
Local Government and Public Involvement in Health Act 2007 to
consider the establishment of Town Councils for Skelmersdale and
Ormskirk.
Ensure that the Review considers, for each
proposed Town Council:



appropriate boundaries;
warding arrangements;
councillor numbers;
governance arrangements;
financial implications and precept
levels;
opportunities for community asset management and
local service delivery;
implementation alongside Local Government
Reorganisation wherever practicable.



Undertake comprehensive public consultation with
residents, businesses, community organisations and other
stakeholders in both towns to ensure that proposals reflect local
aspirations.
Engage with the Ministry of Housing, Communities
and Local Government and those leading Local Government
Reorganisation in Lancashire to ensure that enhanced community
governance forms part of the wider programme of local government
reform.
Receive a report on the outcome of the Community
Governance Review with recommendations for
implementation."

 
An Amendment, circulated prior to the meeting
was moved and seconded.
 
The mover and seconder of the Motion accepted
the Amendment, with the agreement of the meeting.
 
A vote was taken on the Altered Motion, which
was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.   
This Council notes that:

(i)         
The Government’s English Devolution White Paper –
Power and Partnership: Foundations for Growth (December
2024) sets out the most significant programme of local government
reform in over fifty years, combining Local Government
Reorganisation with English devolution. The White Paper makes clear
that these reforms are intended not only to simplify local
government but also to strengthen local democracy and community
empowerment.

(ii)        
The White Paper states:“We know people value the role of
governance at the community scale… We will therefore want to
see stronger community arrangements when reorganisation
happens… We will also rewire the relationship between town
and parish councils and principal local authorities, strengthening
expectations on engagement and community voice.”
(iii)      
The Government has made clear that larger unitary authorities
should be complemented by stronger community governance, ensuring
that local identity and neighbourhood representation are
strengthened rather than diminished.
 
(iv)     
Skelmersdale and Ormskirk are West Lancashire’s two principal
towns, each with its own distinct history, identity, communities
and aspirations, yet neither benefits from an elected town council
dedicated solely to representing its residents and championing its
local priorities.
 
(v)       
In addition, Westhead is the only other area of West Lancashire
without oversight by a parish council.
 
(vi)  Skelmersdale is one of England’s largest
towns without a town council, while Ormskirk, the Borough’s
historic market town and administrative centre, likewise lacks an
elected town council despite its significant civic, cultural and
economic importance.
 
(vii)    
Town and parish councils across England play an increasingly
important role in:
o representing local
communities;
o supporting
regeneration and economic development;
o delivering
neighbourhood services;
o managing community
assets;
o supporting local
organisations;
o improving parks
and public spaces;
o promoting civic
pride and local identity.
 

B.   
That this Council believes that:
(i)             
Local Government Reorganisation must strengthen—not
weaken—local democracy.
(ii)            
As decision-making moves to larger unitary authorities serving
substantially larger populations, there is a compelling need to
ensure that communities continue to have a strong, democratic voice
at the neighbourhood level.
(iii)          
The creation of Town Councils for both Skelmersdale and Ormskirk
and a parish council for Westhead is one way to provide that voice
by creating democratically accountable bodies focused exclusively
on the interests of their respective communities, but other methods
such as the establishment of area committees under the new unitary
council is another method
(iv)          
Such councils or area committees would:

·        
strengthen local democracy and accountability;

·        
enhance community engagement and participation;

·        
support regeneration and economic development;

·        
promote civic identity and local pride;

·        
provide stronger advocacy for local communities;

·        
work in partnership with the future unitary authority to deliver
neighbourhood priorities;

·        
ensure that decisions affecting each town continue to be shaped by
those who know and represent them best.
(v)            
That the current programme of Local Government Reorganisation
presents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to establish governance
arrangements that will serve the people of West Lancashire for
decades to come.
 
C.     That a wide and inclusive initial
public consultation be undertaken with residents, businesses,
community organisations and other stakeholders in both towns and
Westhead to test public support for
(i)   
establishment of new town and parish councils
(ii)  
the alternative establishment of area committees
to ensure that
proposals at the next stage reflect local aspirations.
 
D.        
That the Council engage with the Ministry of Housing, Communities
and Local Government and those leading Local Government
Reorganisation in Lancashire to ensure that enhanced community
governance forms part of the wider programme of local government
reform.

 

E.         
That a report on the outcome of the public consultation undertaken
at 1 above be submitted to full council no later than April 2027,
to allow the Council to make recommendations to the new Shadow
Authority on this council’s preferred option for enhanced
community governance.
topline: The Council has decided to establish town councils for Skelmersdale and Ormskirk to strengthen local democracy and community representation.

content:
The following Altered Motion was moved and
seconded, with the agreement of the meeting:
 
"This Council Notes:
Ormskirk Hospital
is physically located within Lancashire and serves as the principal
acute hospital for West Lancashire, yet its strategic governance
falls under the NHS Cheshire and Merseyside Integrated Care Board
(ICB). Yet the NHS arrangements
affecting the hospital span more than one geography, with the
provider principally aligned to NHS Cheshire and Merseyside
ICB while healthcare services for West
Lancashire residents are commissioned by NHS Lancashire and South
Cumbria ICB.
The government's
upcoming local government reorganisation is expected to establish
new unitary authority structures across Lancashire, creating a
critical window to align public service boundaries.
As West Lancashire
sits outside the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, regional
bodies lack a direct strategic or economic incentive to prioritise
the infrastructure and transport links that support access to
Ormskirk Hospital.
This
Council Believes:
Local
accountability is severely weakened when major health provisions
operate within administrative structures that do not align with
local government borders.
Future healthcare
delivery increasingly depends on the seamless integration of acute
hospital care with adult social care, housing, and public health,
all of which are Lancashire-managed services.
Aligning Ormskirk
Hospital with Lancashire NHS structures would strengthen democratic
oversight, remove unnecessary complexity, and make sure Lancashire
residents have a clear champion within wider strategic
planning.
There is merit in
reviewing whether existing governance and commissioning
arrangements provide West Lancashire residents with an appropriate
voice in decisions affecting their principal acute hospital.
This Council
Resolves:
To formally request
that NHS England together with the Department of Health and Social
Care undertake a comprehensive review of the strategic alignment of
the governance, commissioning and accountability arrangements
affecting Ormskirk Hospital and West Lancashire residents,
assessing whether residents would be better served under Lancashire
NHS strategic and commissioning arrangements.
To seek ironclad
assurances that any future healthcare governance adjustments
reflect the new Lancashire local government structures without
detriment to frontline patient care.
To establish a
cross-party working group to:
·      
gather evidence from residents, healthcare professionals, and
NHS stakeholders regarding the future governance of the
hospital.
·      
submit the findings of that work to NHS England, the Secretary
of State for Health and Social Care and relevant local government
reorganisation bodies.
·      
reaffirm this Council's commitment to protecting and enhancing
healthcare services for West Lancashire residents and ensuring that
local voices are properly represented in decisions affecting those
services.
To request that the
Leader of the Council write to the Chief Executive of NHS England,
the Chief Executives of the relevant Integrated Care Boards
(ICBs), NHS Lancashire and South
Cumbria ICB and NHS Cheshire and
Merseyside ICB, local Members of
Parliament, and the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care
to communicate the contents of this motion and request a formal
response."
 
An Amendment, circulated prior to the meeting
was moved and seconded.
 
A vote was taken on the Amendment, which was
CARRIED.
 
A vote was taken on the Substantive Motion,
which was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 
A.   
That this Council notes:  

(i)         
Ormskirk Hospital is physically located within Lancashire and
serves as the principal acute hospital for West Lancashire, yet its
strategic governance falls under the NHS Cheshire and Merseyside
Integrated Care Board (ICB). 

(ii)        
The government's upcoming local government reorganisation is
expected to establish new unitary authority structures across
Lancashire, creating a critical window to align public service
boundaries. 

(iii)      
As West Lancashire sits outside the Liverpool City Region Combined
Authority, regional bodies lack a direct strategic or economic
incentive to prioritise the infrastructure and transport links that
support access to Ormskirk Hospital. 

 
B.   
This Council Believes:  

(i)             
Local accountability is severely weakened when major health
provisions operate within administrative structures that do not
align with local government borders. 

(ii)            
Future healthcare delivery increasingly depends on the seamless
integration of acute hospital care with adult social care, housing,
and public health, all of which are Lancashire-managed
services. 

(iii)          
Aligning Ormskirk Hospital with Lancashire NHS structures would
strengthen democratic oversight, remove unnecessary complexity, and
make sure Lancashire residents have a clear champion within wider
strategic planning. 

 
C.   
That NHS England be requested to undertake a comprehensive review
of the strategic alignment of Ormskirk Hospital, assessing whether
residents would be better served under Lancashire NHS strategic and
commissioning arrangements. 
D.   
That ironclad assurances be sought that any future healthcare
governance adjustments reflect the new Lancashire local government
structures without detriment to frontline patient care. 

 
E.   
That the Council's commitment to protecting and enhancing
healthcare services for West Lancashire residents and ensuring that
local voices are properly represented in decisions affecting those
services, be reaffirmed.
 

F.   
That the Leader of the Council write to the Chief Executive of NHS
England, the Chief Executives of the relevant Integrated Care
Boards (ICBs), local Members of
Parliament, and the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care,
to communicate the contents of this motion and request a formal
response
topline: The Council has decided to align Ormskirk Hospital with Lancashire NHS structures to strengthen democratic oversight and ensure local residents have a clear champion within wider strategic planning.

content:
The following Motion was moved and
seconded:
 
"Council notes
that:

National reporting has identified
approximately 680 unregulated or illegal children’s care
settings across England and Wales, with a reported 669 children
living in such placements, raising significant safeguarding
concerns.
Unregulated settings operate
outside the regulatory framework of Ofsted, meaning children may
not receive the protections afforded within registered
provision.
Lancashire has one of the highest
concentrations of children’s homes in England, placing
additional pressure on local placement sufficiency and
oversight.
The use of unregulated provision
is widely recognised as a risk factor for vulnerable children,
particularly those with complex needs.

 
Council further
notes:

That responsibility
for children’s social care sits with Lancashire County
Council, but that placement locations within borough boundaries
have direct implications for community safety, safeguarding, and
local services within West Lancashire.

Council resolves to:


Request formally that Lancashire
County Council provide a full breakdown of:

·      
The number of unregulated or unregistered children’s care
settings operating within West Lancashire.
 
·      
The number of children placed in such settings within the
borough.
 
·      
The safeguarding and monitoring arrangements in place
 

2.   Seek assurance from Lancashire
County Council that all children placed within West Lancashire are
appropriately safeguarded and that any unregulated provision is
subject to robust oversight.
 

3.   Write to the Department for
Education expressing concern regarding the national increase in
unregulated placements and requesting clarity on actions being
taken to reduce reliance on such provision.
 

4.   Request a briefing for elected
members on the local impact of unregulated children’s care
provision, including risks, trends, and partnership working
arrangements.

 

5.  Commit to reviewing the
council’s role, in partnership with relevant agencies, in
supporting safeguarding and community awareness where such settings
are located within the borough."
 
A vote was taken, the Motion was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.   
That it be noted that:
 
1)   
National reporting has identified approximately 680 unregulated or
illegal children’s care settings across England and Wales,
with a reported 669 children living in such placements, raising
significant safeguarding concerns.
2)   
Unregulated settings operate outside the regulatory framework of
Ofsted, meaning children may not receive the protections afforded
within registered provision.
3)   
Lancashire has one of the highest concentrations of
children’s homes in England, placing additional pressure on
local placement sufficiency and oversight.
4)   
The use of unregulated provision is widely recognised as a risk
factor for vulnerable children, particularly those with complex
needs.
 

B.   
That it be noted that responsibility for children’s social
care sits with Lancashire County Council, but that placement
locations within borough boundaries have direct implications for
community safety, safeguarding, and local services within West
Lancashire.

C. That Council resolves to:

1)   
Request formally that Lancashire County Council provide a full
breakdown of:

 
(i)   
The number of unregulated or unregistered children’s care
settings operating within West Lancashire.
 
(ii)  
The number of children placed in such settings within the
borough.
 
(iii)The safeguarding and
monitoring arrangements in place
 
2)   
Seek assurance from Lancashire County Council that all children
placed within West Lancashire are appropriately safeguarded and
that any unregulated provision is subject to robust oversight.
 
3)   
Write to the Department for Education expressing concern regarding
the national increase in unregulated placements and requesting
clarity on actions being taken to reduce reliance on such
provision.
 
4)   
Request a briefing for elected members on the local impact of
unregulated children’s care provision, including risks,
trends, and partnership working arrangements.
 
5)   
Commit to reviewing the council’s role, in partnership with
relevant agencies, in supporting safeguarding and community
awareness where such settings are located within the borough.
topline: The Council has decided to address safeguarding concerns by requesting information, seeking assurance, and committing to reviewing their role in supporting vulnerable children in unregulated care settings.

purpose:
This report seeks approval for the governance,
delivery arrangements and required delegations for the Pride in
Place Programme in Skelmersdale South East (Digmoor). It outlines
Government expectations, the establishment of a Neighbourhood Board
with an Independent Chair and the Council’s role as
Accountable Body. The report details consultation approaches,
programme timescales, funding allocations, the development of a
ten-year Regeneration Plan and associated resource, financial and

arrangements outlined in the report.

That the Director of Planning, Economy & Wellbeing be granted
delegated authority to review and formally accept the

conditions and capacity funding.

granted delegated authority to establish the Skelmersdale
South East (Digmoor) Pride in Place Neighbourhood Board (the
Board). Thereafter in conjunction with the Board to take all
necessary steps to implement, govern and administer the scheme to
include but not limited to establishing the Neighbourhood Board,
requesting changes to the boundary, developing the Regeneration
Plan, programme management, technical expertise and other
activities in accordance with Government guidance.

East (Digmoor) Pride in Place
Neighbourhood Board be given delegated authority to develop a
Regeneration Plan for submission to Government, including
undertaking public consultation, subject to authorisation by the
Director of Finance & Resources (Section 151 Officer) prior to
submission.

That the Director of Planning, Economy & Wellbeing be given
delegated authority to undertake a public consultation in relation
to the Pride in Place Programme for Skelmersdale South East (Digmoor).

purpose:
This report provides an overview of the
Government’s consultation on the proposed reforms to the
National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) and associated changes to
the wider planning system, published on 16 December 2025. The
consultation, which runs until 10 March 2026, seeks views on a
revised NPPF aimed at creating a clearer, more consistent and more
rules-based planning framework.

It includes significant structural changes separating plan-making
and national decision-making policies, updates to housing delivery,
sustainable development, climate change policy, and the role of
local plans. The consultation also addresses related areas such as
data centres and on-site energy generation, standardised viability
inputs, and site threshold reforms. The report summarises the key
proposals and sets out their potential implications for the
Council’s planning functions.

Council’s agreed leisure transformation programme.

to the meeting, was moved and seconded.

was CARRIED.

existing Leisure Facilities Project allocation monies within the

deliver feasibility, design and technical work for future delivery

of Park Pool.

subsequently bring back further reports to the Leisure Operations
Working Group and full Council, in April, detailing the preferred
option, associated costs, delivery route, timescales and funding
strategy and before any planning submission or external funding
application is made.

Ormskirk will be delivered as Phase 2 of the leisure transformation
programme following Local Government Reorganisation once new
provision has been provided in Skelmersdale.

Wellbeing to bring a Report to the next Meeting of the Full Council
setting out the programme of essential repairs for both Nye Bevan
and Park Pool centres, to ensure continued operation for the coming
5 years.

content:
The following Motion was moved and
seconded:
 
"That this council
notes the outstanding results in the report by His Majesty’s
Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services
(HMICFRS) on Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service (LFRS).
In August this year
the HMIFRS published LFRS report on how well they are performing.
LFRS were measured against 11 areas and given a grade for each
including understanding risk and protecting the public through fire
regulation. Six areas were measured as outstanding and five areas
as good.
No other Fire
Service has been measured so highly.
 
This council
resolves to:

Write to congratulate the Chief
Fire Officer of Lancashire Fire & Rescue Service and the Chair
of Lancashire Combined Fire Authority on the well-earned report and
thanking all officers for their service in keeping Lancashire
safe.
Write to Ormskirk, Skelmersdale
and Tarleton Fire Station and congratulate them on an outstanding
report and thank all Lancashire Fire & Rescue Service personnel
in West Lancashire for keeping us safe.

 
For information
Link to the HMICFRS report

Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service 2023–2025 - His
Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue
Services"
 
A vote was taken, the Motion was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.   
That this council notes the outstanding results in the report by
His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire &
Rescue Services (HMICFRS) on Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service
(LFRS).In August this year the HMIFRS published LFRS report on how
well they are performing. LFRS were measured against 11 areas and
given a grade for each including understanding risk and protecting
the public through fire regulation. Six areas were measured as
outstanding and five areas as good. No other Fire Service has been
measured so highly.
 

B.   
That this council:
 
1.    
Write to congratulate the Chief Fire Officer of Lancashire Fire
& Rescue Service and the Chair of Lancashire Combined Fire
Authority on the well-earned report and thanking all officers for
their service in keeping Lancashire safe.
 
2.    
Write to Ormskirk, Skelmersdale and Tarleton Fire Station and
congratulate them on an outstanding report and thank all Lancashire
Fire & Rescue Service personnel in West Lancashire for keeping
us safe.
topline: The Council has decided to note the outstanding results in the report by HMICFRS on Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service and to congratulate and thank the personnel for their service.

content:
The followng
Motion was moved and seconded:
 
Council notes:

That animals given as prizes suffer
greatly and there are documented poor outcomes. Many goldfish, for
example die from stress, temperature shock, poor handling or oxygen
starvation.
That winning an animal as a prize
encourages impulsive ownership rather than the careful planning
that pets require and new owners may not have the knowledge or
resources to provide proper care.
That all councils in Wales have
banned the practice of giving live animals as prizes on council
land and that over 160 councils in England have also done so.
That the RSPCA support councils in
implementing an outright ban on the giving of live animals as
prizes in any form and encourage them to request the Government to
implement a nationwide ban on this practice.

 
Council resolves to:

Implement an outright ban on the
giving of live animals as prizes in any form on West Lancashire
Borough Council land from 1 November 2025.
Change procedure to ensure that,
where a licence from West Lancashire Borough council is required
for an event or undertaking, a condition of the licence is that the
giving of live animals as prizes is prohibited
Communicate this change to Parish
and Town Councils in West Lancashire and encourage them to
implement a similar ban on all events taking place on land they may
own
Communicate this change via WLBC
channels eg social media
Instruct the Acting Chief Executive
to write to the UK Government urging an outright ban on the giving
of live animals as prizes on public and private land

 
A vote was taken,
the Motion was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.   
That Council notes:
(i)    
That animals given as prizes suffer greatly and there are
documented poor outcomes. Many goldfish, for example die from
stress, temperature shock, poor handling or oxygen starvation.
(ii)   
That winning an animal as a prize encourages impulsive ownership
rather than the careful planning that pets require and new owners
may not have the knowledge or resources to provide proper care.
(iii)  
That all councils in Wales have banned the practice of giving live
animals as prizes on council land and that over 160 councils in
England have also done so.
(iv)  
That the RSPCA support councils in implementing an outright ban on
the giving of live animals as prizes in any form and encourage them
to request the Government to implement a nationwide ban on this
practice.
 

B.   
That Council resolves to:
(i)    
Implement an outright ban on the giving of live animals as prizes
in any form on West Lancashire Borough Council land from 1 November
2025.
(ii)   
Change procedure to ensure that, where a licence from West
Lancashire Borough council is required for an event or undertaking,
a condition of the licence is that the giving of live animals as
prizes is prohibited
(iii)  
Communicate this change to Parish and Town Councils in West
Lancashire and encourage them to implement a similar ban on all
events taking place on land they may own
(iv)  
Communicate this change via WLBC channels eg social media
(v)   
Instruct the Acting Chief Executive to write to the UK Government
urging an outright ban on the giving of live animals as prizes on
public and private land
topline: The Council has decided to implement an outright ban on the giving of live animals as prizes on council land, following recommendations from the RSPCA and other councils.

content:
The following Motion was moved and
seconded:
 
"This council notes:
 
Local government has endured
central government funding cuts of more than 50% since 2010.
Between 2010 and 2020, councils lost 60p out of every £1 they
have received from central government. Research by UNISON has shown
that councils across England, Wales and Scotland are facing a
collective funding shortfall of more than £4bn by the
financial year 2024/25 and a cumulative funding gap of £8bn
by 2025/26. The last Government’s ‘levelling up’
pots of money did little to help.
 
Council and school workers kept
our communities safe through the pandemic, often putting themselves
at considerable risk as they work to protect public health, provide
quality housing, ensure our children continue to be educated, and
look after older and vulnerable people.
 
Since 2010, the local
government workforce has endured years of pay restraint with the
majority of pay points losing at least 25 per cent of their value
since 2009/10. Staff have endured the worst cost of living crisis
in a generation.
 
At the same time, workers have
experienced ever-increasing workloads and persistent job
insecurity. Across the UK, 900,000 jobs have been lost in local
government since June 2010 – a reduction of more than 30 per
cent. Local government has arguably been hit by more severe job
losses than any other part of the public sector. There has been a
disproportionate impact on women, with women making up more than
three-quarters of the local government workforce.
 
Recent research shows that if
the Government had fully fund the unions’ 2025 pay claim,
around half of the money would be recouped thanks to increased tax
revenue, reduced expenditure on benefits and tax credits, and
increased consumer spending in the local economy.
 
This council
believes:
 
1. Local government workers
keep our communities clean and safe, look after those in need and
keep our towns and cities running.
 
2. Without the professionalism
and dedication of our staff, the council services our residents
rely on would not be deliverable.
 
3. Local government workers
deserve a proper real-terms pay increase. The Government needs to
take responsibility and fully fund this increase; it should not put
the burden on local authorities whose funding has been cut to the
bone and who were not offered adequate support through the Covid-19
pandemic.
 
This council resolves
to:
 
A. Call on the Local Government
Association to make urgent representations to central government to
fund the NJC pay claim
 
B. Write to the Chancellor and
Secretary of State to call for a pay increase for local government
workers to be funded with new money from central
government
 
C. Meet with local NJC union
representatives to convey support for the pay claim and consider
practical ways in which the council can support the 2026/27
campaign
 
D. Encourage all local
government workers to join a union."
 
A vote was taken, the Motion
was CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED:
 

A.    
That this council notes:
 
(i)    
Local government has endured central government
funding cuts of more than 50% since 2010. Between 2010 and 2020,
councils lost 60p out of every £1 they have received from
central government. Research by UNISON has shown that councils
across England, Wales and Scotland are facing a collective funding
shortfall of more than £4bn by the financial year 2024/25 and
a cumulative funding gap of £8bn by 2025/26. The last
Government’s ‘levelling up’ pots of money did
little to help.

 
(ii)   
Council and school workers kept our communities safe
through the pandemic, often putting themselves at considerable risk
as they work to protect public health, provide quality housing,
ensure our children continue to be educated, and look after older
and vulnerable people.

 
(iii) 
Since 2010, the local government workforce has
endured years of pay restraint with the majority of pay points
losing at least 25 per cent of their value since 2009/10. Staff
have endured the worst cost of living crisis in a
generation.

 
(iv) 
At the same time, workers have experienced
ever-increasing workloads and persistent job insecurity. Across the
UK, 900,000 jobs have been lost in local government since June 2010
– a reduction of more than 30 per cent. Local government has
arguably been hit by more severe job losses than any other part of
the public sector. There has been a disproportionate impact on
women, with women making up more than three-quarters of the local
government workforce.

 
(v)  
Recent research shows that if the Government had
fully fund the unions’ 2025 pay claim, around half of the
money would be recouped thanks to increased tax revenue, reduced
expenditure on benefits and tax credits, and increased consumer
spending in the local economy.

 

B.    
That this council believes:
 
(i)    
Local government workers keep our communities clean
and safe, look after those in need and keep our towns and cities
running.

 
(ii)   
Without the professionalism and dedication of our
staff, the council services our residents rely on would not be
deliverable.

 
(iii) 
Local government workers deserve a proper real-terms
pay increase. The Government needs to take responsibility and fully
fund this increase; it should not put the burden on local
authorities whose funding has been cut to the bone and who were not
offered adequate support through the Covid-19 pandemic.
 

C.   
That this council resolves to:
 
(i)    
Call on the Local Government Association to make
urgent representations to central government to fund the NJC pay
claim

 
(ii)   
Write to the Chancellor and Secretary of State to
call for a pay increase for local government workers to be funded
with new money from central government

 
(iii) 
Meet with local NJC union representatives to convey
support for the pay claim and consider practical ways in which the
council can support the 2026/27 campaign

 
(iv) 
Encourage all local government workers to join a
union.
 
(Note: Councillors Gagen, West,
Furey, Coughan and Hesketh left the room whilst this item was under
consideration.)
topline: The Council has decided to address funding cuts and pay restraints for local government workers in the UK.
